report.answer_text:
Chancellor Rachel Reeves delivered the budget on 26 November 2025.
Tax rises
The budget set out policies to raise £26 billion in taxes, an all-time high.[1]
The freeze on personal tax thresholds was extended from April 2028 to April 2031.[2]
A council tax charge, widely called a "mansion tax", was introduced on properties valued over £2 million.[3]
A £2,000 cap on salary sacrifice pension contributions will start in 2029.[3]
The annual cash ISA limit is being cut to £12,000[4]. This figure comes from a Financial Times report that MoneyWeek cited before the speech, so check it against the final detail.
A new 3p per mile levy on electric vehicles was announced. The electric car grant will be extended until 2030.[5]
Reeves said she would not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher or additional rates of income tax, or VAT.[4]
Spending and household costs
The two-child benefit cap was scrapped, at an expected cost of around £3 billion according to the OBR.[5] The change takes effect from April 2026.[2]
Energy bills will fall by an average of £150 from April 2026. The saving comes from removing the previous government's "Eco scheme" levy.[5]
Regulated rail fares will be frozen.[5]
The minimum wage for 18–20 year olds will rise 8.5% to £10.85 an hour. For apprentices aged 16–17 it will rise 6% to £8 an hour.[5]
£300 million of new capital investment will go into NHS technology.[5]
Business and investment
The annual limits on venture capital schemes will double.[3]
New listings will get a three-year exemption from stamp duty reserve tax.[3]
Fiscal position
The OBR said fiscal "headroom" against Reeves's own rules will rise to £22 billion by the end of the decade. Reeves had envisaged about £10 billion at her last budget.[3]
The OBR's forecast was accidentally leaked before the speech in a "technical error".[4]
For the full detail, the Which? summary and the Wikipedia article are good places to start.
